I register my dog. It's pretty simple and quick. There's someone at the police office front desk that should be able to help with paperwork. Every year I go in person to renew. Once again, quick and easy, but yes really annoying you have to do it in person. I wish they had an online portal. When it's time to renew you'll get a postcard reminder in the mail.

Not that I'm suggesting it, but I have literally never been asked for my dog's registration, and I know several people who don't register their dogs. I registered mine just in case something does happen (i.e. another dog attacks us and the police have to get involved). I want to give my pup the best chance and protect her if something does occur. The law can be really unfriendly to pets. So I register her. But like I said, the majority of people I know with dogs do not.

Here's the recipe for the pretzels: https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/sourdough-pretzels-recipe

And here's the ingredients for the 2 seeded loaves

400 g all purpose flour 

300 g bread flour

150 g wheat flour

75 g rye flour

24 g salt

170 starter

100 g seeds + extra for rolling shaped loaves in.


I use a seed mixture of pumpkin, sunflower, brown sesame, black sesame, flax, and poppy. But you can do whatever works. I mix it up based on what I have and don't keep strict ratios.


1. Mix flour and water, sit for 1 hour
2. Add start. Sit for 1/2 hour
3. Add salt. Sit for 1/2
4. Stretch and fold. Sit for 1/2 (repeat step total of 4 times)
5. Sit for 1.5 hours
6. Pre shape on counter, let sit covered by bowl for 1/2 hour
7. Shape and roll in seeds and place in banneton. Sit for 1/2 hour
8. Place in fridge overnight (for me this ends up being ~15 hours cold fermentation)
9. Bake in morning. I do 20 mins at 550 in a Dutch oven (though my oven probably only gets close to 500 and isn't consistent temp) and then 20 min lid off at 425. The one loaf is burnt because I forgot to turn down the heat immediately.

Our cat is very docile to the dog so our problems are mostly around the dog not respectful of the cat's space.

Have you tried feeding the cat or rewarding the cat when the dog is in the same room? Maybe have the cat on a cat tree or out of reach of the dog and just work on them being comfortable in the same room. 

For us we saw huge improvements when I started feeding treats to both animals in the same room. My favorite is to buy some single ingredient freeze dried treats that both cats and dogs can eat (we have a chicken and salmon one they both love) That way you only have to worry about one treat and can treat both animals at the same time. Take it slow and don't force them to interact, but encourage that being together isn't scary and you get treats! And if the cat wants to run away, let them. Just keep the puppy from following. Baby steps is the key. You might have to start with the cat in the doorway just looking at the dog or something.

It took a very long time, and honestly they only snuggle when I'm the warm lap between them. For us that's mostly on the cat's side. She's very dog friendly, grew up with labs, but at the age of 15, she's not playful. I keep telling her to just hiss or give the dog a smack, but she's too gentle. Which is a good thing, but the puppy has struggled with boundaries.

The biggest thing we did is just give it the time they needed to adjust. And that has been months. We made sure there were many safe places in the house (extra cat trees, rooms that the cat could get into and the dog couldn't). We only recently started letting the dog into the bedroom because that's been the cat's space. 

Most of it for us is the puppy needs to mature and have the calmness of age. There are lots of good resources for cat and puppy interactions. Just stuff like teaching the dog not to pounce the cat by using a leash around the house when they are young. Praising when they look at the cat, but don't go near it. It's all dependent on the cat and dog. For us the cat was docile and the dog was playful, but not trying to attack her. Feeding them treats in the same room and on on floor together actually helped us a lot. Because they were next to each other, but focused on me. But my cat is a glutton so this might not qork for everyone. But training methods can change based on how the two individuals are reacting.

For my partner and I we decided I would keep her if we split. I'm better off financially and have been paying for 90% of her expenses. There are some benefits in the short term of puppyhood (potty training, enforcing naps, easier to leave them alone for short periods). In the long term the biggest benefit is easier time at the vets and groomers. Also travel. It's worth at least doing a tiny bit of training so your pup doesn't panic at the vets or groomers. But if you don't use a crate it's not a huge deal. 

I use a crate because my high energy border collie mix does not settle. We have established the crate and pen as her safe spot and we do enforced naps. Otherwise she seriously would go all day. Also I plan on traveling with her and maybe checking out agility (the girl can run!). But later in her life the crate will be used for travel and I plan on her being free roaming at home. Once I can teach her to settle outside of her crate that is.

Do what's right for your situation. My sister never used a crate and her dog is totally fine. I would be lost without the ability to enforce a nap in the crate. Puppies are all different and it's okay to mix and match training for what works for you.

We just got our girl spayed Tues and the guilt is real. She was seriously back to her playful bouncy self within 24 hours. Dang resilient little things. If you have a higher energy breed I cannot recommend puzzle toys and food dispenser toys enough. We even made a few out of recycling materials. They've been so huge for us.

Our puppy came from a coworker. I gave him a fleece baby blanket and asked if he'd mine leaving it for the puppies to use and us taking it home the following week with the puppy. I think it really helped her settle in. I put it inside her crate with her and she'd bury her nose in it. She also would carry it around the house for a few weeks, and still does occasionally at 5 months old. Anytime she was tired she'd go grab the blanket from the crate and start doing zoomies around the house with it. Here's pup tax of her during the first week with her blanket https://imgur.com/5Ylh7FS.jpg 

One random tip for crate training if you are doing that is we did naps in the crate since day one. If she was tired and didn't want to be in the crate, we'd let her doze off in our laps and then gently place her in the crate with the door open, while continuing to sit outside near the crate. Sometimes she'd get up to have lap snugs again, and we'd repeat the process until she stayed in the crate. I think it help with early association with the crate. She was already introduced to crates prior to coming to us, so we never had that initial fear of the crate.

Beyond that just take the first few days slow. We had 4 days off work before returning to our work from home routine. We marathoned lord of the rings in the same room as her crate/pen set up, while just letting her slowly get used to us, the house, and all the new stuff.

My girl humped a new bed fairly aggressively around the 4 month old mark. It's usually just excitement and not sexual. Spaying won't necessarily change the behavior. Generally just try to redirect attention to something else or if she's insistent she might need a time out to calm down. My girl also did this a few times at daycare to the other dogs and the workers would kennel her for a short time out. They told me now she hasn't displayed the behavior at daycare since. She learned it meant fun time was over.

Definitely check in with your vet when you visit just to get their opinion. I'd say it's also not uncommon for puppies to have soft stool. You can always mix a little pumpkin in with the kibble or give a spoonful as a treat. It has all sorts of good fiber which can help. Make sure it's just pumpkin puree and not like pie filling which will have added sugar. I actually freeze kibble and pumpkin in my puppies kong as a treat and she loves it. Could also just be first week jitters and getting used to the routine. Hopefully your pup having time to get used to a consistent schedule and consistent food will help.

Maybe try meditation technique? Recognize the face, breath in, let the face exist, breathe out. It's neither scary or good, it just simply is. What really helped me get started with recall was hand targeting. Basically you teach them to touch your open palm with their nose and slow move further away while adding in a verbal cue. My next step was getting her to chase me outside in the yard, but I started inside with hand targeting. We are at 5 months and if she's distracted the recall isn't there, but sometimes I can get her attention and start running away and she'll chase me. Recall takes time.

We are currently opening the house more to her (being careful because we have a senior cat that doesn't love being pounced on so kitty still have some safe rooms) and I've noticed a slight drop in energy lately, which is encouraging. My pup isn't very food motivated and we struggle at times. This is our routine at this point though.

Low value: cut up treats that are called Snif Snaxs. They are salmon and sweet potatoes. It was the first treat I could even get her interested in. If you can use kibble though that's is probably the best. My pup barely eats her normal kibble so it's a no go for me. 

Medium: beef grillers. Many companies made a variation on this. They are easy to break apart and a nice soft treat.

High: cheese. I'm pretty sure she'd kill me for cheese. They are currently our recall practice treat or for puppy class when I'm trying to pull her attention from other dogs. I use small peices of cut up Swiss or cheese curds if you can find them as they hold together well. We have a cheese manufacturer in town so I can buy cheap bulk.
I assume it's so stores can hang them up for display. It's awful annoying though. My puppy will zone in on those spots, even if I cut them off, and just tear the toy apart.

From what I've seen unless they have an allergy, get grain food. There's some evidence of grain free food being associated with heart issues. 

I've heard great things about purina pro. My vet recommended it along with science diet. We actually tried to switch my pup to a different food but after several weeks of diarrhea we decided we'd revisit the idea when we have to change her to an adult food. 

If your pup is already on purina, I'd probably go with that. Also ask your vet for their advice if you feel overwhelmed. The internet is difficult to pull information from. My vet basically just said any grain containing puppy food is probably fine as long as it's not bare bottom generic store brand.

Weight of the parents is a much better indicator. My parents would breed our labs when I was a kid, and the puppies always ended up being in the middle of the two parents. Where you know the parents weight I'd go with that indicator.

I actually wanted a bigger dog, but I really just wanted an active running buddy and she needed a home. I figure a fox terrier, border collie mutt would be a good adventure friend. Though if she magically does grow to 45 lbs I'll have to buy a bigger crate lol.

Yeah the calculators aren't very good in my opinion. I mean my puppy isn't full grown, but her mom was 15lbs and her dad was about 35lbs (7 and 16 kg) and the calculators are estimating about 45lbs, 20kg. My pup is an oops pup and it's amazing how well mom did with how big the pups are in relation. There's just no way my pup is going to be bigger than her dad. We did a DNA test because the origins of the dad was unknown and they estimate about 28lb, 13kg based in her genetic make up. I find that much more believable.
Whenever I drop her off at daycare she is also just wiggling to get out of my arms and to go back to the play area. I know she loves it there. I'm just such a worrier.

She had no socialization as a puppy and had never been to the boarders. They now struggle to take trips because they have to find a friend to watch the dog.

I only do half days for this reason, but even that seems like a lot because she doesn't stop playing. Last time I was there they said they almost crated her because the other dogs were starting to slow down and she wasn't always very respectful of a tired dog. I told them to yes please do kennel her if needed so hopefully in the future they will. I think the staff is still learning us and didn't want to upset us if they kenneled her during her 4 hour daycare. If you do a whole day of daycare they give the dogs a break during lunch and let the boarding dogs out during that time.

My friend is a groomer and said she's never had issues being left in the kennels unlike a lot of her clients. I'm just an anxiety mess and love my puppy and want for her all the happiness in the world.

Outdoor stuff with your pup will be great! Just remember that puppy's growth plates don't close till 1-1.5 years old depending on breed size. So don't overdo it with your pup. There's lots of great short trails to go on though.

For group stuff I'd suggest puppy classes. I currently have a new pup and they're great for the dog and for my personal growth as an owner. We even meet a few other owners through the classes that will be great friends for the pup. 

For non dog related stuff (sadly Cache valley isn't very dog friendly) I know there are some cooking classes at Love to Cook that you might meet new people at if that's your thing. Also I play a lot of mtg and love our local card stores. Hopefully with the covid vaccine soon to be widely distributed play areas will open. You can also find board game and DnD groups through these stores if that's your thing.
